```{python}
#| tags: [setup]
import sys, os
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.abspath("."))
from _pcpkg import *  # noqa: F401,F403
import doe_report as D
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.stats as sstat

DOC = "PCR-008"
UO = "aex"
UO_TITLE = "Anion Exchange Chromatography (Step 8)"

# --- doc-local derived scalars (pulled from the model; never typed) -----------------
# Run structure and centre-point replication.
n_scr = doe_runs(UO, "screening")
n_rsm = doe_runs(UO, "rsm")
n_cp_scr = int(D.center_cv_df(UO, "screening").iloc[0]["n"])
n_cp_rsm = int(D.center_cv_df(UO, "rsm").iloc[0]["n"])

RESPS = D.responses(UO)                       # measured DoE responses
GOV_CQAS = [r for r in RESPS if D.acceptance_for(UO, r) is not None]  # responses with a criterion

# Commercial-scale capability accessors (capability.csv is exposed as `cap`).
_capi = cap.set_index("key")
def cpk(k):   return float(_capi.loc[k, "Cpk"])
def cmean(k): return float(_capi.loc[k, "mean"])
def csd(k):   return float(_capi.loc[k, "sd"])
def clo(k):   return float(_capi.loc[k, "acc_low"])
def chi(k):   return float(_capi.loc[k, "acc_high"])

# Nominal modular viral-clearance contributions (viral_clearance.csv).
_vc = csv("viral_clearance.csv").set_index("step")
aex_mvm   = float(_vc.loc["Anion Exchange (AEX)", "MVM"])
aex_xmulv = float(_vc.loc["Anion Exchange (AEX)", "XMuLV"])

# RSM fit cache + accessors (reused across Results, Design space, Capability).
_fits = {r: D.fit(UO, "rsm", r) for r in RESPS}
def fs(resp, k): return _fits[resp][k]
pred_hcp_xmulv_min = min(fs("hcp_out_ng_mg", "predR2"), fs("xmulv_lrf", "predR2"))

# Screening effect accessor (term = coded label, e.g. 'A', 'B', 'AB', 'BD').
def eff(resp, term, superseded=False):
    return D.screening_effects_df(UO, resp, superseded=superseded).set_index("Term").loc[term]

# Step-level (back-calculated) viral-clearance floors.
def vfloor(resp): return D.acceptance_for(UO, resp)[0]

# Parameter set-point / NOR / characterization-range formatters.
def sp(f):  return f"{CFG.unit_op(UO).param(f).setpoint:g}"
def nor(f):
    p = CFG.unit_op(UO).param(f); return f"{p.nor[0]:g}–{p.nor[1]:g}"
def pr(f):
    p = CFG.unit_op(UO).param(f); return f"{p.prange[0]:g}–{p.prange[1]:g}"
def unit(f): return CFG.unit_op(UO).param(f).unit

# p-value formatter (grounds the value; renders the conventional threshold at the tail).
def pf(p):  return "< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"
```

# Executive summary {.unnumbered}

This report documents the Stage 1 (Process Design) characterization of the A-Mab
anion-exchange (AEX) polishing step, the flow-through operation that follows cation-exchange
polishing and is the final chromatographic step of the drug-substance purification train. The
study was executed against the paired plan PCP-008 on a qualified commercial-equivalent
scale-down model, under the lifecycle approach to process validation [@fda2011; @pdatr60;
@ispegpg2023], the enhanced quality-by-design paradigm [@ichq8; @ichq9; @ichq11], and —
because the step carries part of the viral-safety claim — the viral-clearance evaluation
framework of ICH Q5A(R2) [@ichq5a], all grounded in the A-Mab case study [@amab2009]. Anion
exchange is the step at which the process establishes the minute-virus-of-mice (MVM,
parvovirus) clearance claim — the only CQA it sets — while providing orthogonal
enveloped-virus (XMuLV) clearance and a further reduction of host-cell protein (HCP), residual
DNA and leached Protein A.

Five process parameters were characterized. Load pH, equilibration/wash-1 conductivity, load
conductivity and protein load were studied together in a `{python} n_scr`-run two-level
full-factorial screening design and a `{python} n_rsm`-run face-centred central-composite
response-surface design; operating flow rate was assessed univariately. The screening design
identified the significant factors and two-factor interactions; the response-surface design
then quantified main effects, interactions and curvature and defined the multivariate
operating region. All four multivariate factors and the flow rate are classified as
well-controlled critical process parameters (WC-CPP); the step has no key process parameter
and no parameter requiring the most stringent (full CPP) control.

The MVM and XMuLV clearance surfaces and the pool-HCP surface are governed by the
electrostatic environment: MVM log-reduction rises with load pH (effect
`{python} f"{eff('mvm_lrf','A')['Effect']:.2f}"` log₁₀, p `{python} pf(eff('mvm_lrf','A')['p-value'])`)
and falls with load conductivity, and the pool-HCP level is set by load pH and wash-1
conductivity acting in opposition. The response-surface models are adequate over the
characterized region (no significant lack of fit); the pool-HCP and XMuLV models are
additionally predictive (predicted R² ≥ `{python} f"{pred_hcp_xmulv_min:.2f}"`), while the MVM
model is adequate (R² = `{python} f"{fs('mvm_lrf','R2'):.2f}"`) with a more modest predicted R²
that reflects the narrower log-reduction range of the parvovirus spiking assay.

Anion exchange contributes approximately `{python} f"{aex_mvm:.2f}"` log₁₀ of MVM clearance at
the nominal condition — the first and principal MVM-clearance step — so that the drug substance
meets its ≥ `{python} f"{clo('lrv_mvm'):g}"` log₁₀ cumulative MVM requirement (achieved
cumulative `{python} f"{V['total_lrv_mvm']:.1f}"` log₁₀, Cpk = `{python} f"{cpk('lrv_mvm'):.2f}"`).
This MVM capability is the tightest of the entire drug substance (process-minimum Cpk
`{python} f"{V['min_cpk']:.2f}"`), yet retains margin above the requirement. The step
contributes `{python} f"{aex_xmulv:.2f}"` log₁₀ to the cumulative XMuLV claim (Cpk =
`{python} f"{cpk('lrv_xmulv'):.2f}"`) alongside low-pH inactivation and virus filtration, and
holds pool HCP well within its ≤ `{python} f"{chi('hcp'):g}"` ng/mg limit (Cpk =
`{python} f"{cpk('hcp'):.2f}"`). The step does not, by itself, deliver the cumulative
viral-safety claim: MVM safety depends jointly on this step and virus filtration (PCR-009), and
XMuLV safety on low-pH inactivation (PCR-006) and virus filtration.

Three deviations were recorded, investigated and impact-assessed. The most consequential — a
non-representative, deamidated load in the first DoE execution — invalidated that execution for
operating-region definition; the affected designs were re-executed in full on a requalified,
representative load, and the analysis reported here is that requalified execution. None of the
three deviations altered the parameter classifications or the operating region defined below.
The step is well understood and robust across the characterized ranges, and the parameter
classifications, operating region and control contributions defined here are carried forward
into the master report PCMR-001.

# Introduction

## Product and unit operation

A-Mab is a humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody whose primary mechanism of action is
antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity; it is manufactured by the platform
drug-substance train summarized in @tbl-train and purified by the sequence Protein A → low-pH
viral inactivation → cation exchange → anion exchange → virus filtration → UF/DF [@amab2009].
Anion exchange (Step 8) is the final polishing chromatography of that train.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(process_steps_df())
```

: A-Mab drug-substance process train (Steps 3–10) and each step's principal control-strategy role. {#tbl-train}

The step is operated in flow-through mode: the cation-exchange eluate is titrated and
conditioned to the target load pH and conductivity and passed over a strong anion-exchange
resin under conditions at which the antibody carries a slight net positive charge and does not
bind, while the more acidic host-cell protein, DNA, leached Protein A and model viruses are
retained. The product is therefore recovered in the flow-through and wash and the impurities
and viruses are removed by binding — a mechanism that makes the step a high-recovery polish
rather than a yield-limiting capture. Anion exchange forms no product quality attribute; it
sets one CQA of its own, the cumulative MVM (parvovirus) viral-clearance claim, and contributes
clearance of enveloped virus and of the process impurities that are formed upstream. This
division of labour — one CQA set, several cleared — is developed in @sec-prior and is the reason
the step is characterized against both a viral-clearance criterion and the drug-substance
impurity specifications.

## Objectives

The characterization had five objectives, mirroring the paired plan PCP-008: (i) to quantify
the relationships between the anion-exchange process parameters and the step's viral-clearance,
impurity-clearance and yield responses; (ii) to define the multivariate operating region over
which the governed attributes remain within acceptance; (iii) to establish the proven
acceptable range of each parameter and locate the normal operating range within it; (iv) to
classify each parameter according to its demonstrated criticality; and (v) to justify the
Stage-2 operating ranges and the step's contribution to the overall control strategy for
transfer to commercial manufacture.

## Regulatory and scientific basis

The study follows the lifecycle approach to process validation, in which Stage-1 process design
establishes the process understanding on which the later qualification and continued
verification stages depend [@fda2011; @pdatr60; @ispegpg2023]; the report is organized to map
onto the Stage-1 process-design report of PDA Technical Report 60. Criticality is treated as a
continuum rather than a binary [@ichq9]: a parameter's classification reflects the magnitude of
its demonstrated effect on the CQAs and the width of the range over which that effect keeps the
attribute in specification, consistent with the enhanced, quality-by-design development approach
[@ichq8; @ichq11]. Because anion exchange is one of three orthogonal viral-clearance steps, its
clearance data are additionally evaluated within the ICH Q5A(R2) framework [@ichq5a], and its
contribution is credited modularly rather than claimed in full (@sec-control). The controlled
documents that govern the study and its sibling documents are listed in @tbl-related.

# Prior knowledge and quality risk basis {#sec-prior}

## Platform and prior-product knowledge

Flow-through anion-exchange polishing is a platform operation whose behaviour is well
established from related humanized IgG1 antibodies (X-Mab, Y-Mab and Z-Mab) and from A-Mab
clinical and engineering experience [@amab2009]; the characterization therefore confirms and
bounds a known mechanism rather than discovering a new one. Prior knowledge established that, in
flow-through mode, the binding of impurities and virus is governed by the electrostatic
environment. A higher load pH increases the net negative charge of the acidic impurities and of
the model viruses, strengthens their retention on the positively charged resin and therefore
improves their clearance, while raising the equilibration/wash-1 or the load conductivity
screens that electrostatic attraction and weakens retention. The antibody itself, at a pH below
its isoelectric point, remains weakly positive and transmits across the studied range, so the
step is expected to be high-recovery and largely yield-insensitive to the chromatographic
factors. These expectations set the direction of every factor before the study and are the
hypotheses the results confirm or refute.

## Quality attributes in scope

The attributes governed by anion exchange are listed in @tbl-cqa-scope: the one CQA the step
sets and the four it clears, each with its drug-substance acceptance criterion and criticality.
The step sets the cumulative MVM clearance — a very-high-criticality viral-safety attribute —
and clears the cumulative XMuLV clearance (also very high criticality) together with three
process impurities of lower criticality (HCP, residual DNA and leached Protein A). Criticality
here follows the case-study risk tool: the two viral-safety attributes carry the highest
severity, which is why the viral responses, not the impurity responses, are the binding
constraints on the operating region and on capability.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(cqas_by_keys(["lrv_mvm", "lrv_xmulv", "hcp", "residual_dna", "leached_protein_a"]))
```

: Quality attributes governed by anion exchange — one set (MVM) and four cleared. {#tbl-cqa-scope}

## Risk-based prioritization and parameter selection

The parameters carried into this study, and the ranges over which they were varied, were set by
the pre-characterization risk assessment RA-001, which risk-ranked the anion-exchange
parameters and filtered them to those with a credible impact on the governed attributes. Four
parameters — load pH, equilibration/wash-1 conductivity, load conductivity and protein load —
act directly on the electrostatic clearance mechanism and were therefore studied jointly in the
multivariate design, so that their interactions could be resolved rather than assumed absent.
Each factor's range was set wider than its intended normal operating range to characterize the
knowledge space around the set-point: the load-pH range brackets the titration tolerance of the
conditioned load, the two conductivity ranges bracket buffer-preparation and load-conditioning
variability, and the protein-load range extends to a resin loading well above the intended
set-point to probe the mass-transfer limit of impurity and virus binding. Operating flow rate
was judged to act on clearance only through residence time and not through the binding
chemistry, and was therefore assessed univariately rather than consuming a factor in the
multivariate design. Consistent with the conservative default for a very-high-criticality
attribute, the viral responses were characterized across the full factor ranges even where
prior knowledge predicted robustness.

# Materials and methods

## Scale-down model and its qualification

The characterization was performed on a scale-down model of the anion-exchange step operated at
commercial-equivalent conditions — the same resin chemistry, bed height, load ratio and linear
flow velocity as the intended commercial operation — in accordance with the step operation
procedure (SOP-2011) and the scale-down-model qualification procedure (SOP-1001). The model was
qualified by matching its input and output attributes to at-scale development data across the
operating point: the flow-through-pool impurity levels, the step yield and the viral
log-reduction factors of the qualified model reproduced the at-scale values within the
analytical variability of the respective methods, establishing that the model is representative
for both operating-range and clearance claims. For the viral responses the model is a qualified
small-scale spiking model, in which a defined titre of XMuLV or MVM is spiked into the
conditioned load and the log-reduction factor is measured across the step under the ICH Q5A(R2)
expectation that small-scale clearance data support the cumulative claim [@ichq5a]. The
replicated centre point of each design provides the pure-error estimate against which lack of
fit is tested (@sec-results); its reproducibility is reported in @tbl-center.

## Operation

Each run conditioned the cation-exchange eluate to its target load pH and load conductivity,
equilibrated the column and performed the post-load wash at the target wash-1 conductivity, and
collected the flow-through and wash as the product pool under UV-triggered pool-collection
control. Inputs held to platform specification — resin lot and packing quality, column
geometry, buffer identities and the sanitization regime (SOP-2008) — were identity- and
quality-controlled rather than characterized, so that the measured responses reflect the studied
factors and not uncontrolled operational variation. The single exception is the charge-variant
quality of the load material, which is a feed-input attribute that proved consequential to the
study and is treated explicitly under Deviations (@sec-dev) and in the control strategy
(@sec-control).

## Analytical methods

The validated methods used to measure the step's responses are listed in @tbl-sop. Pool HCP was
measured by ELISA (AMV-3012), residual DNA by qPCR (AMV-3014) and leached Protein A by ELISA
(AMV-3016); the enveloped- and small-virus log-reduction factors were measured by the XMuLV and
MVM infectivity assays (AMV-3017 and AMV-3018); and the charge-variant quality of the load,
central to the load-material deviation, was measured by imaged capillary isoelectric focusing
(AMV-3013). Method performance is not reproduced here; the reportable ranges and techniques are
summarized in Appendix D.

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(sop_table(sops=AEX_SOP_REFS, amvs=AEX_AMV_REFS))
```

: Controlled procedures and validated analytical methods for the anion-exchange characterization. {#tbl-sop}

## Sampling plan

Each design run yielded one flow-through pool, sampled for HCP, residual DNA, leached Protein A
and step yield, with viral log-reduction determined on the spiked runs. The screening design
carried `{python} n_cp_scr` replicated centre points and the response-surface design carried
`{python} n_cp_rsm`, providing the independent pure-error replication used for the lack-of-fit
test. Load-material charge-variant quality was verified on each load lot by icIEF prior to
execution, the control that ultimately detected the non-representative load in the first
execution.

## Statistical methods

Factors were analysed in coded units (set-point = 0, characterization edges = −1 and +1). The
screening data were fitted by ordinary least squares with all main effects and two-factor
interactions, each effect estimate being twice the corresponding coded coefficient; the
response-surface data were fitted with the full quadratic model. Significance was assessed at
α = 0.05. Model adequacy was judged by the coefficient of determination and its adjusted and
predicted (PRESS-based) forms, the overall F-test, and an ANOVA partition of the residual into
lack-of-fit and pure-error components using the replicated centre points; a response with no
statistically active factor is reported as robust rather than modelled. Commercial-scale
capability was estimated by Monte-Carlo simulation of `{python} f"{V['n_monte_carlo']:,}"`
batches with each parameter drawn across its normal operating range and propagated through the
fitted response-surface models, from which the one-sided process-capability index (Cpk) of each
governed attribute was computed.

## Factors, ranges and the knowledge space

The five characterized parameters, their set-points, normal operating ranges, characterization
ranges and final classifications are given in @tbl-params, and the coded legend for the four
multivariate factors in @tbl-legend. Each characterization range extends beyond the normal
operating range so that the knowledge space is bounded on both sides of the set-point: load pH
was varied over `{python} pr('load_ph')` around a `{python} sp('load_ph')` set-point,
equilibration/wash-1 conductivity over `{python} pr('wash1_cond')` mS/cm, load conductivity over
`{python} pr('load_cond')` mS/cm and protein load over `{python} pr('load')` g/L resin. The
range column is the characterization range and not a proven acceptable range; the proven
acceptable ranges are computed per attribute in @sec-par.

## Screening design

The four multivariate factors were first studied in a two-level full-factorial screening design
of `{python} n_scr` runs, including `{python} n_cp_scr` replicated centre points, resolving all
four main effects and all six two-factor interactions clear of one another. The screening
design's role is to identify which factors and interactions are active; the magnitudes it
returns are refined by the subsequent response-surface model. The full coded design matrix and
responses are in Appendix A.

## Response-surface design

The same four factors were then studied in a face-centred central-composite design of
`{python} n_rsm` runs — the factorial points, the axial (face) points that add curvature, and
`{python} n_cp_rsm` replicated centre points — fitted with the full quadratic model. This
response-surface model is the predictive, design-space-defining model of the study: it
quantifies the main effects, two-factor interactions and curvature and is the basis for the
operating region (@sec-ds) and the proven acceptable ranges (@sec-par). The full coded matrix
and responses are in Appendix B.

## Univariate assessment

Operating flow rate was assessed univariately across `{python} pr('flow')` cm/hr about its
`{python} sp('flow')` cm/hr set-point rather than in the multivariate design, because it
influences clearance only through residence time and not through the binding chemistry that
couples the other four factors; treating it separately avoids inflating the multivariate design
without loss of information. Its assessment confirmed that clearance and recovery are
insensitive to flow rate over the studied range, and it is classified from that univariate
evidence in @sec-class.

# Results {#sec-results}

## Centre-point performance and reproducibility

The replicated centre point establishes the pure-error baseline for the study, and its
reproducibility is attribute-dependent (@tbl-center). The viral log-reduction factors and the
step yield are highly reproducible at the centre point (%CV of
`{python} f"{D.center_cv_df(UO,'rsm').iloc[1]['%CV']:.1f}"`% for XMuLV,
`{python} f"{D.center_cv_df(UO,'rsm').iloc[2]['%CV']:.1f}"`% for MVM and
`{python} f"{D.center_cv_df(UO,'rsm').iloc[3]['%CV']:.1f}"`% for yield), whereas the pool HCP is
the least precise response (%CV `{python} f"{D.center_cv_df(UO,'rsm').iloc[0]['%CV']:.1f}"`%),
consistent with the near-baseline HCP levels this polishing step delivers and with the ELISA's
variability at low analyte concentration. This higher HCP variance is carried through to the
lack-of-fit test and is the reason HCP effects near the assay's precision are hedged below.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(D.center_cv_df(UO, "rsm"))
```

: Centre-point reproducibility of the response-surface design (pure-error basis). {#tbl-center}

## Screening: factor effects

The screening design resolved a small number of large, mechanistically coherent effects and
found the remaining terms inactive (@tbl-scr-summary); the effect estimates for pool HCP are
detailed in @tbl-scr-hcp, and the viral and yield responses are described below with their full
effect tables in Appendix C. Two factors dominate every governed response, and they are the two
the mechanism predicts.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(D.fit_summary_df(UO, "screening"))
```

: Screening-model adequacy across the four responses. {#tbl-scr-summary}

The pool HCP is governed by load pH and equilibration/wash-1 conductivity acting in opposite
directions: a higher wash-1 conductivity raises the pool HCP (effect
`{python} f"{eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','B')['Effect']:.1f}"` ng/mg, p
`{python} pf(eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','B')['p-value'])`, poorer clearance) and a higher load pH lowers
it (effect `{python} f"{eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','A')['Effect']:.1f}"` ng/mg, p
`{python} pf(eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','A')['p-value'])`, better clearance), with a significant load-pH ×
wash-1-conductivity interaction (effect `{python} f"{eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','AB')['Effect']:.1f}"`
ng/mg, p `{python} pf(eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','AB')['p-value'])`) that means conductivity matters most
at low load pH. Notably, the protein load has no significant effect on pool HCP in this
representative-load design (effect `{python} f"{eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','D')['Effect']:.2f}"` ng/mg,
p `{python} pf(eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','D')['p-value'])`), and its interaction with wash-1
conductivity is likewise absent (effect `{python} f"{eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','BD')['Effect']:.2f}"`
ng/mg, p `{python} pf(eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','BD')['p-value'])`) — a result that becomes central to
the load-material deviation in @sec-dev, because that same interaction was large and significant
in the invalidated first execution.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(D.screening_effects_df(UO, "hcp_out_ng_mg"))
```

: Screening effect estimates for pool HCP (requalified-load execution). {#tbl-scr-hcp}

The viral responses share a single governing direction. Both the MVM and XMuLV log-reductions
rise with load pH (MVM effect `{python} f"{eff('mvm_lrf','A')['Effect']:.2f}"` log₁₀, p
`{python} pf(eff('mvm_lrf','A')['p-value'])`; XMuLV effect
`{python} f"{eff('xmulv_lrf','A')['Effect']:.2f}"` log₁₀, p
`{python} pf(eff('xmulv_lrf','A')['p-value'])`) and fall with load conductivity (MVM effect
`{python} f"{eff('mvm_lrf','C')['Effect']:.2f}"` log₁₀, p `{python} pf(eff('mvm_lrf','C')['p-value'])`;
XMuLV effect `{python} f"{eff('xmulv_lrf','C')['Effect']:.2f}"` log₁₀, p
`{python} pf(eff('xmulv_lrf','C')['p-value'])`), exactly as the electrostatic mechanism predicts —
stronger binding of the negatively charged virus at higher pH and lower ionic strength. The step
yield shows no significant dependence on any factor, consistent with a high-recovery flow-through
operation in which the antibody transmits regardless of the chromatographic condition. These
screening magnitudes are indicative; the design-space magnitudes are taken from the
response-surface models.

## Response-surface models

The response-surface models are adequate across the characterized region and, for the two
principal clearance responses, additionally predictive (@tbl-rsm-summary). The pool-HCP and
XMuLV models carry predicted R² of `{python} f"{fs('hcp_out_ng_mg','predR2'):.2f}"` and

and is reported as robust rather than modelled. Because the MVM model sets the step's CQA, its

## Mechanistic interpretation

The surfaces look as they do because a single physical mechanism governs the step. At the
operating pH the antibody carries a slight net positive charge and transmits, while the more
acidic host-cell protein, DNA, leached Protein A and model viruses carry net negative charge and
bind the positively charged resin; the strength of that binding, and therefore the clearance, is
set by the electrostatic environment. Raising the load pH increases the net negative charge of
the impurities and virus and strengthens their retention, so the pool HCP falls and the XMuLV
and MVM log-reductions rise; raising the wash-1 or the load conductivity screens the charge
interaction and weakens retention, so the pool HCP rises and the viral log-reductions fall. The
significant load-pH × wash-1-conductivity interaction on HCP is the expected coupling of these
two levers — the conductivity penalty is largest where the pH is lowest and the binding already
weakest. This is precisely why the impurity and viral load are assured over a multivariate
operating region rather than by independent one-dimensional ranges: the acceptable value of any
one factor depends on where the others sit, and only a joint region captures that dependence.
The absence of a protein-load effect on clearance, over a range extending well above the
set-point loading, further indicates that the binding capacity for impurities and virus is not
exhausted at the intended load and that the load-related risk lies in the charge-variant quality
of the feed rather than in a load set-point.

# Design space {#sec-ds}

The anion-exchange design space is a multivariate region in the four well-controlled critical
process parameters — load pH, equilibration/wash-1 conductivity, load conductivity and protein
load — over which the governed attributes remain within acceptance. Its principal planes are the
two the mechanism dictates: the load-pH × wash-1-conductivity plane that governs pool HCP, and
the load-pH × load-conductivity plane that governs the XMuLV and MVM log-reductions. Within the
characterized ranges the impurity and viral optima coincide toward the high-pH, low-conductivity
corner, so the region has no interior trade-off; its binding constraints are the corners at
which a viral log-reduction is lowest — low load pH combined with high load conductivity — which
is the worst case the region must still satisfy, and at which the MVM contribution remains above
its back-calculated step floor of `{python} f"{vfloor('mvm_lrf'):.2f}"` log₁₀.

The normal operating range of each parameter lies well inside this characterized region, which
in turn lies inside the broader knowledge space bounded by the proven acceptable ranges of
@sec-par: load pH is operated at `{python} nor('load_ph')` within a characterized
`{python} pr('load_ph')`, wash-1 conductivity at `{python} nor('wash1_cond')` within
`{python} pr('wash1_cond')` mS/cm, load conductivity at `{python} nor('load_cond')` within
`{python} pr('load_cond')` mS/cm, and protein load at `{python} nor('load')` within
`{python} pr('load')` g/L resin. Movement within this operating region is not a change and
requires no assessment, whereas movement outside it would be evaluated under the quality system
[@amab2009; @ichq8]. The claim is bounded to the characterized factor ranges and to the fitted
response-surface models, and rests on the qualification of the scale-down model and its
small-scale viral-spiking model (@sec-results); it is not extrapolated beyond the studied edges.

# Proven acceptable ranges {#sec-par}

The proven acceptable range (PAR) of each parameter complements the multivariate design space
with a per-attribute, per-parameter view: the sub-range of a parameter's characterization range
over which a given CQA stays within its acceptance criterion. The acceptance basis differs by
attribute type and is returned by the model rather than assumed. For pool HCP the criterion is
the drug-substance specification (≤ `{python} f"{chi('hcp'):g}"` ng/mg); for the viral-clearance
attributes the criterion is the step-level required log-reduction, back-calculated from the
cumulative requirement minus the clearance credited to the other steps —
`{python} f"{vfloor('mvm_lrf'):.2f}"` log₁₀ for MVM and `{python} f"{vfloor('xmulv_lrf'):.2f}"`
log₁₀ for XMuLV — reflecting the modular nature of the viral-safety claim. Each parameter is
reported with two proven acceptable ranges (@tbl-par): the at-set-point PAR, holding the other
factors at their set-points, and the NOR-propagated PAR, in which the other factors vary within
their normal operating ranges by Monte-Carlo of the fitted response-surface model — the
reproducible, more conservative robustness criterion.

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(D.par_table(UO))
```

: Proven acceptable ranges for each governed CQA × parameter — characterization range and both the at-set-point and NOR-propagated PARs. {#tbl-par}

Across every governed CQA and every multivariate parameter the two proven acceptable ranges
coincide with the full characterization range (@tbl-par): the at-set-point and NOR-propagated
PARs each span the entire studied range, for pool HCP, XMuLV and MVM alike. The interpretation is
strong and specific. Each parameter's whole characterization range is proven acceptable for every
governed attribute, and remains acceptable even when the other factors co-vary within their
normal operating ranges — so no single parameter, moved alone or with the rest of the operating
point drifting within the NOR, drives any attribute out of specification anywhere in the studied
space. The representative PAR plots make this visible for each governed CQA and its governing
factor (@fig-par-hcp, @fig-par-xmulv, @fig-par-mvm): the acceptable region, shaded, covers the
full parameter axis in both the at-set-point and the NOR-propagated panel, with the set-point and
normal operating range marked well inside it.

The relationship to the design space is therefore explicit. The proven acceptable ranges are
univariate, NOR-robust statements about one parameter at a time; the design space is the
multivariate region that captures the joint dependence among the factors. Because each univariate
PAR already spans the full characterization range, the binding constraint on the operating region
is not any single-parameter PAR but the multivariate worst-case corner identified in @sec-ds —
the low-pH, high-conductivity corner at which the viral log-reduction is lowest. This conclusion
is bounded to the characterized ranges and the fitted models: it states that no univariate
excursion within the studied space breaches acceptance, not that the parameters may be moved
without limit.

# Process capability and robustness {#sec-cap}

The commercial-scale capability of every governed attribute meets its acceptance criterion with
margin (@tbl-cap), estimated by Monte-Carlo simulation of `{python} f"{V['n_monte_carlo']:,}"`
batches with each parameter drawn across its normal operating range and propagated through the
fitted response-surface models. The MVM clearance — the CQA the step sets — is the tightest
capability of the entire drug substance: its one-sided Cpk of `{python} f"{cpk('lrv_mvm'):.2f}"`
is the process minimum (`{python} f"{V['min_cpk']:.2f}"`), yet the simulated cumulative MVM
clearance (`{python} f"{cmean('lrv_mvm'):.1f}"` ± `{python} f"{csd('lrv_mvm'):.2g}"` log₁₀) sits
above its ≥ `{python} f"{clo('lrv_mvm'):g}"` log₁₀ requirement, to which anion exchange
contributes its `{python} f"{aex_mvm:.2f}"` log₁₀ as the first and principal MVM-clearance step
alongside virus filtration (PCR-009). The XMuLV clearance is comparably capable (Cpk =
`{python} f"{cpk('lrv_xmulv'):.2f}"`, cumulative `{python} f"{cmean('lrv_xmulv'):.1f}"` log₁₀
against a ≥ `{python} f"{clo('lrv_xmulv'):g}"` log₁₀ requirement), to which this step contributes
`{python} f"{aex_xmulv:.2f}"` log₁₀ orthogonally to low-pH inactivation (PCR-006) and virus
filtration. The pool HCP is highly capable (Cpk = `{python} f"{cpk('hcp'):.2f}"`, mean
`{python} f"{cmean('hcp'):.1f}"` ng/mg against a ≤ `{python} f"{chi('hcp'):g}"` ng/mg limit),
with residual DNA and leached Protein A far inside their limits (Cpk =
`{python} f"{cpk('residual_dna'):.1f}"` and `{python} f"{cpk('leached_protein_a'):.0f}"`), the
latter cleared here after its principal removal at Protein A capture (PCR-005) and cation exchange
(PCR-007). The two viral capabilities are the binding ones; the impurity capabilities carry ample
margin. These estimates are bounded to the normal operating ranges and to the scale-down and
small-scale spiking models, and the cumulative viral figures are consolidated across the three
orthogonal viral steps in PCMR-001, not claimed by this step alone.

```{python}

```

# Parameter classification {#sec-class}

Each parameter is classified from its demonstrated effect on the governed attributes and the
risk it carries within the operating region; the classifications are summarized in @tbl-params
and justified below.

- **Load pH — WC-CPP.** The dominant lever on both viral log-reductions and, with wash-1
  conductivity, on pool HCP; it is therefore controlled as a well-controlled critical process
  parameter, at `{python} sp('load_ph')` within a `{python} nor('load_ph')` normal operating
  range. Its whole characterization range is a proven acceptable range for every governed CQA
  (@sec-par), so the residual risk is fully managed by the routine pH control the NOR represents.
- **Equilibration/Wash-1 conductivity — WC-CPP.** The governing factor for pool HCP and, with
  load pH, a determinant of impurity clearance; controlled as a WC-CPP at
  `{python} sp('wash1_cond')` mS/cm within `{python} nor('wash1_cond')`. Its effect is
  significant but its proven acceptable range spans the full studied range, so the attribute
  stays in specification across the NOR.
- **Load conductivity — WC-CPP.** The secondary lever on the viral log-reductions, acting in the
  opposite direction to load pH; controlled as a WC-CPP at `{python} sp('load_cond')` mS/cm
  within `{python} nor('load_cond')`. It defines, with load pH, the worst-case corner of the
  viral design space, which is why it is controlled rather than treated as a general parameter
  despite its smaller effect.
- **Protein load — WC-CPP.** Carries a credible risk to the impurity and viral load and is
  therefore controlled as a WC-CPP; in representative-quality load material it showed no
  significant effect on clearance or recovery over a range extending well above the set-point, so
  its acceptable range is wide. The characterization localized the load-related risk to the
  charge-variant quality of the load material (@sec-dev), which is controlled as a feed-input
  attribute rather than by a load set-point.
- **Operating flow rate — WC-CPP.** Assessed univariately and found to have no significant effect
  on clearance or recovery over `{python} pr('flow')` cm/hr; it is nonetheless controlled as a
  WC-CPP at `{python} sp('flow')` cm/hr within `{python} nor('flow')`, because residence time
  carries a credible mechanistic risk to a binding-limited clearance step and a wide, evidenced
  acceptable range is the appropriate control rather than declassification.

No parameter at this step required the most stringent (full CPP) control, and the step carries no
key process parameter: all five parameters are well-controlled critical process parameters, each
with a demonstrated effect and an evidenced acceptable range.

# Contribution to the control strategy {#sec-control}

Anion exchange contributes to the control strategy as the process's principal parvovirus-
clearance step and as a polishing step for enveloped virus and process impurities. Its
contributions are: control of the four multivariate WC-CPPs and the flow rate to the normal
operating ranges of @tbl-params; in-process monitoring of the flow-through-pool HCP by ELISA
(AMV-3012) and UV-triggered pool collection at the corrected set-point established under
@sec-dev; verification of the load-material charge-variant quality by icIEF (AMV-3013) as a
feed-input control, added as a direct consequence of the load-material deviation; and the resin
life-cycle, packing and sanitization controls of SOP-2008. The MVM clearance the step sets is
credited toward the cumulative viral-safety claim modularly, alongside the orthogonal
contributions of low-pH inactivation (PCR-006) and virus filtration (PCR-009); the
enveloped-virus and impurity clearances are likewise partial contributions to attributes also
controlled upstream at Protein A capture (PCR-005) and cation exchange (PCR-007). The step does
not, by itself, guarantee the cumulative viral-safety claim or the release-level impurity
attributes: its role is to provide an orthogonal, robust clearance increment whose consolidation
with the other steps is performed in the master report PCMR-001.

# Discussion

The characterization establishes that the anion-exchange step is well understood and robust
across the studied ranges, and that its behaviour is the behaviour prior platform knowledge
predicted. A single electrostatic mechanism accounts for every governed response: load pH and
conductivity set the strength of impurity and virus binding, the impurity and viral optima
coincide, and the step is high-recovery and insensitive to protein load and flow rate over wide
ranges. The response-surface models are adequate over the characterized region and, for pool HCP
and XMuLV, additionally predictive; the more modest predicted R² of the MVM model is attributable
to the narrower dynamic range of the parvovirus spiking assay against its reproducibility, not to
model inadequacy, and the MVM classification and design space rest on its strong, highly
significant main effects and its non-significant lack of fit. Confidence in these conclusions
rests on the qualification of the scale-down model, whose input and output attributes matched
at-scale development data, and on the qualified small-scale viral-spiking model.

Three deviations were recorded, and their treatment is summarized adverse-first in @sec-dev. The
most consequential was a non-representative, deamidated load in the first DoE execution, which —
through an anomalous protein-load × wash-1-conductivity interaction — drove the flow-through pool
out of its in-process limit at the high-load/high-conductivity corner; because an operating
region cannot be defined on a non-representative load, the affected designs were invalidated and
re-executed in full on a requalified load, and the requalified execution is the analysis reported
throughout this document. The two remaining deviations — a permissive UV pool-collection
set-point common to both executions, and a single wash-buffer lot released slightly below its pH
range — were bounded by argument and, respectively, corrected by modelling and verification runs
and retained. The principal limitations of the study are those inherent to Stage-1
characterization: the reliance on a scale-down model, the use of a small-scale viral-spiking
model whose log-reduction range is narrower than the cumulative claim it supports, and the
assessment of resin performance over a limited number of cycles rather than the full life-cycle.
Each is managed forward — the scale-down and spiking models by their qualification and by
confirmation at scale, and the resin life-cycle by the controls of SOP-2008 and by continued
process verification. No parameter required control more stringent than the well-controlled
critical designation, which is the appropriate outcome for a step whose attributes remain in
specification across their full proven acceptable ranges.

# Conclusions

The anion-exchange polishing step is well characterized, well understood and robust across the
ranges studied. A multivariate operating region in the four well-controlled critical process
parameters was defined over which the governed attributes remain within acceptance; the proven
acceptable range of each parameter spans its full characterization range and is robust to NOR
co-variation, so the binding constraint on the operating region is the multivariate worst-case
corner rather than any univariate range. Every governed attribute meets its commercial-scale
acceptance criterion with margin, the tightest being the MVM clearance the step sets (Cpk =
`{python} f"{cpk('lrv_mvm'):.2f}"`, the process minimum), which anion exchange establishes as the
first and principal parvovirus-clearance step alongside virus filtration. The three recorded
deviations were investigated, impact-assessed and resolved without altering the parameter
classifications or the operating region. The step does not by itself deliver the cumulative
viral-safety claim; its contribution is consolidated with the other viral and polishing steps in
the master report PCMR-001, into which the classifications, operating region and control
contributions defined here are carried forward.

# Deviations from the plan {#sec-dev}

Three deviations were recorded during execution; each was investigated, its root cause
established, and its impact on the reported conclusions assessed (@tbl-dev). One invalidated the
first DoE execution and forced a full re-execution, one was a set-point correction common to both
executions, and one was a single out-of-range buffer lot retained on a bounded-impact argument.
None altered the parameter classifications or the operating region defined above.

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(dev_register(DOC))
```

: Recorded deviations for the anion-exchange characterization. {#tbl-dev}

## DEV-008-01 — Non-representative (deamidated) load; designs invalidated and re-executed

In the first execution of the screening and response-surface designs, the anion-exchange load —
the cation-exchange eluate — was subsequently found to carry an elevated acidic charge-variant
(deamidation) burden of `{python} f"{dev_008_01_acidic_variants_deamidated_pct:g}"`% by icIEF
(AMV-3013), against `{python} f"{dev_008_01_acidic_variants_requalified_pct:g}"`% for
representative material, the result of an out-of-trend extended neutralized hold of
`{python} f"{dev_008_01_neutralized_hold_h:g}"` hours (lot LOT-CEX-8842) that promoted asparagine
deamidation. In that first execution, at the high-protein-load / high-wash-1-conductivity corner
of the design, the flow-through-pool HCP rose sharply above its in-process action limit and the
pool purity became unacceptable, through an anomalous protein-load × wash-1-conductivity
interaction that is absent from representative material. In the invalidated data the protein-load
main effect and its interaction with wash-1 conductivity are both large and significant (effects
`{python} f"{eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','D',superseded=True)['Effect']:.0f}"` and
`{python} f"{eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','BD',superseded=True)['Effect']:.0f}"` ng/mg, p
`{python} pf(eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','BD',superseded=True)['p-value'])`; @tbl-scr-hcp-sup). Because an
acceptable operating region cannot be defined on a non-representative load, the affected screening
and response-surface designs were invalidated for operating-region definition and re-executed in
full on a requalified, representative load.

The root cause is confirmed by the requalified data. In the requalified-load design reported
throughout this document, the protein-load × wash-1-conductivity interaction is statistically
absent (effect `{python} f"{eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','BD')['Effect']:.2f}"` ng/mg, p =
`{python} f"{eff('hcp_out_ng_mg','BD')['p-value']:.2f}"`; @tbl-scr-hcp) and the protein-load main
effect is likewise non-significant. The anomalous interaction seen in the first execution was
therefore an artifact of the degraded (deamidated) load — whose additional acidic charge variants
competed for the resin and coupled the protein load to the wash conductivity — and not an
intrinsic property of the step. The disposition is that the superseded dataset is retained and
referenced for this root-cause confirmation only; the reported analysis, classifications and
operating region derive entirely from the requalified execution. The deviation also generated a
standing feed-input control: the load-material charge-variant quality is verified by icIEF before
the step (@sec-control).

```{python}
#| output: asis
show(D.screening_effects_df(UO, "hcp_out_ng_mg", superseded=True))
```

: Pool-HCP screening effects from the invalidated first execution (superseded; shown for root-cause confirmation only). {#tbl-scr-hcp-sup}

## DEV-008-02 — Permissive trailing-edge UV pool-collection set-point

In both executions the trailing-edge UV set-point that stops pool collection was set slightly
permissive, at `{python} f"{dev_008_02_uv_pool_stop_original_mau:g}"` mAU rather than the intended
`{python} f"{dev_008_02_uv_pool_stop_corrected_mau:g}"` mAU, and was detected on post-execution
pool-fraction reconciliation against the HCP assay (AMV-3012). Because the identical set-point was
applied to every run, its effect is a common-mode offset: it shifts the absolute
flow-through-pool HCP level by an approximately constant amount but does not change the factor
effects, the two-factor interactions or the geometry of the operating region, since adding a
constant to every response changes only the model intercept and not the coefficients. The
parameter classifications and the design-space geometry reported here are therefore unaffected;
only the absolute in-process pool-collection set-point required correction. The set-point was
corrected to `{python} f"{dev_008_02_uv_pool_stop_corrected_mau:g}"` mAU and the correction
verified by `{python} f"{dev_008_02_ver_n:g}"` confirmation runs at the corrected set-point plus
`{python} f"{dev_008_02_ver_robust_n:g}"` robustness runs, which bounded the corrected pool-HCP
level with a relative 95% confidence half-width of `{python} f"{dev_008_02_ci_hw:g}"`%. The
corrected set-point is the one carried into the control strategy (@sec-control).

## DEV-008-03 — Equilibration/Wash-1 buffer released below its pH range

On one screening run the equilibration/wash-1 buffer lot (LOT-BUF-8815) was released at a
measured pH of `{python} f"{dev_008_03_buffer_ph_measured:g}"`, below its
`{python} f"{dev_008_03_buffer_ph_low_limit:g}"` lower acceptance limit and its
`{python} f"{dev_008_03_buffer_ph_target:g}"` target, detected on buffer release testing per
SOP-2103; the root cause was a titration-endpoint error at buffer preparation. The deviation was
retained. Flow-through clearance at this step is governed by the load pH and the wash-1
conductivity, not by the wash-buffer pH per se, and the small buffer-pH offset falls well within
the load-pH range the study characterized, so the affected run remains representative of the
operating region and does not alter the fitted effects. The impact assessment therefore brackets
the excursion within the studied space and confirms that no re-execution of the run was required.
